He accuses him of having abandoned knowledge and preached instead not-comprehending and faith. He sees in him a rhetorician who can write orthographically, form periods, and rival Nicolai — who was actually Fichte's fiercest opponent — in clarity of shallow comprehensibility. Fichte as oxygen and Nicolai as hydrogen, united, would give the true water of the age. He defends the enthusiasts against him and says on p. 156: "When I recall the many soulful and heartfelt utterances of our Leibniz, Kepler, and many others — all of which, according to Mr. Fichte, would have to be considered nonsense — I cannot help but consider that he has shown himself to be the most spiritless and heartless of all philosophers who have made a name for themselves." He even accuses him — which seems to me the strongest charge against Fichte — of cowardly cleverness. He remained, he says, obligated to the proof that Schelling had misunderstood him. P. [ ]: "It remained at silence, which at the same time afforded several advantages. It spared the trouble of setting against the allegedly misunderstood system the correctly understood one, which would remove all misinterpretations — with which one risked, at the present time, only entangling oneself further and talking oneself in deeper. There might indeed here and there still be some good-natured soul who interpreted the silence as noble contempt (although otherwise no opponent seemed too lowly for Mr. Fichte to instruct); or as a fruitful and pregnant lull before a storm, of which one could not possibly foresee that it would dissolve into as gentle a rain as it now has in the Blessed Life." P. 163: "I call upon every honest man and thinker to say whether Mr. Fichte's attack on natural philosophy was not conducted behind his opponent's back and by stealth, such that the latter must still turn around, face the following crowd, and say: it is I whom he has wounded. We have stood against him in honest, open combat, with scientific weapons and in scientific form, before the eyes of the thinking men of our nation. He carries out his blows against us before Berlin ladies, privy councillors, merchants, and the like; in the dark of a private lecture he scatters slanders against those who cannot defend themselves, until

Schelling, by contrast, depicted with an ironic tinge how he, because he had grasped the ungodly in its nullity, necessarily had to be hated and persecuted by an age which — as Fichte had said in the Characteristics — is the age of absolute sinfulness. P. 149: "The appearance of a doctrine which denies all existence of the ungodly, in an age whose morality rests on precisely this existence, must necessarily produce, within that age itself, quite peculiar moral effects, at which only the ignorant can be surprised. Would we be right in what we say of the morality of the age, if our doctrine were not combated in the most immoral way, on grounds of morality, by people who display toward us themselves the greatest lack of morality — for the honor of their moral doctrine? What have we ourselves posited as the two poles of life?

Die heilige Sitte von der einen; die religiöse Begeiſterung von der andern Seite. Eben dieſe aber ſind, ausgeſtorben und Bertilgt in der herrſchenden Lehre und Biloung, „und an ihre Stelle iſt etwas getreten, das von beiden nichts enthält, und beide von ſich ausſchließt.

Sacred custom on the one side, religious enthusiasm on the other. But these very things have died out and been extinguished in the prevailing doctrine and culture, and in their place has stepped something that contains neither of the two, and excludes both from itself.

Der Menſch, dem mein Ohr und meine Thür verschlossen iſt, kann doch hingeben und mich of: fentlid verläumden; und er kann wiſſen, daß id es weiß, ohne daß er doch nöthig -bat vor mir zu er: röthen.“

Can it then surprise us that our doctrine feels first of all the wildness of the age directed against it, and must it not calmly bear the consequences thereof and accept them as just so many proofs of the truth of what it asserts about the character of present-day morality? Can I myself be surprised that I have now for a long time here and there still been opposed with arguments, but in general have become a target of lies, malice, and personal persecution? Have I not richly deserved all this? Have I not, according to occasion and circumstance, done much ill to the base and spiritless, not spared Pharisees and hypocrites, stripped the sheep's clothing from many of them and unmasked their inner deceit? So too have I always been heartily averse to sentimentality of every kind, and have thereby betrayed my wicked heart clearly enough. Had I counted on principles of honor, I would be doubly served right: for I ought indeed to have known that inner dishonor confesses itself without fear of disgrace, and that nothing harms it when it is exposed as such. The man to whom my ear and my door are closed can nonetheless go about and slander me publicly; and he can know that I know it, without having any need to blush before me."

p. 282

Gegen das Ende hin: erhebt Schelling ſeinen [p. 282] prophetiſchen Ton; die neue Erkenntnißart wird ver: kündet; das Aufhören aller Geſchiedenheit der Sdu: len und Meinungen; die Schwärmer werden gelobt; er verſpricht ihre Schriften zu studiren; nicht aus Berachtung, sondern aus tabelnswerther Nachläſſigkeit habe er dies bisher verabſáumt.

Toward the end Schelling raises his prophetic tone; the new mode of knowledge is proclaimed; the cessation of all division of schools and opinions; the enthusiasts are praised; he promises to study their writings, having neglected this until now not out of contempt but out of blameworthy negligence.

Es werden auch ei: nige Anſáße gemacht, den reßigen Fichte von dem früheren zu unterſceiden, aber der Gedanke, daß derſelbe die Ideen der Naturphiloſophie über Gott, Religion und Sittlichkeit an ſich bringen wolle, tritt der Friedensunterhandlung immer zu ſtörend ents gegen. Dieſes Proceſſiren über das Mein und Dein iſt einmal ein Grundzug bei Schelling. S. 99 be: bauptet er auch, daß Fichte die Deutung des Fd als das logos aus ſeiner, Schelling's, Schrift: Philoſo: phie und Religion S. 41 entlehnt habe. . Dies kann nicht hindern, zu vermuthen, daß aus Schelling Fichte nicht bloß von der Periode der Wiſſenſchaftslehre der, ſondern auch aus eben der von ihm bekämpften Per riode Manches verdanke.

Some attempts are also made to distinguish the present Fichte from the earlier one, but the thought that this same Fichte wishes to appropriate the ideas of natural philosophy concerning God, religion, and morality always intrudes too disruptively upon the peace negotiations. This litigating over "mine" and "thine" is indeed a basic trait in Schelling. On p. 99 he also claims that Fichte borrowed the interpretation of the I as the Logos from his own, Schelling's, work Philosophy and Religion, p. 41. This cannot prevent one from suspecting that Schelling too owes much to Fichte — not only from the period of the Wissenschaftslehre, but also from precisely the period he was now combating.

But we must guard against letting our insight into these spoil the enjoyment of what is genuinely excellent — as so easily happens with narrow-minded people, who graze on the self-feeling of their superiority in uttering blame, and who, to keep this titillation alive in themselves, generally prefer to blame rather than to praise. And just as little as we have let polemic rest in our critique, just as little do we wish to deny apology its due, and we gladly recognize this address as a genuine masterpiece. Its title, admittedly, is poorly chosen. It should read: Some Ideas on Nature and Art.

[p. 285] Dieſe Probleme waren ſeit Lessing's Laokoon und Winkelmann's Geſchichte der Kunſt vielfach ventilirt worden. Göthe hatte in den Propyläen viel zur Berichtigung dieſer Begriffe zu wirken geſucht und in ſeiner Biographie Winkelmanns 1805 war ein ge wisser Abidluß der ganzen Bewegung eingetreten, deſſen Ruhe auch Schellinge Abhandlung durchdringt.

These problems had been much debated since Lessing's Laocoön and Winckelmann's History of Art. Goethe, in the Propyläen, had sought to do much to correct these concepts, and in his 1805 biography of Winckelmann a certain conclusion of the whole movement had been reached, whose calm also pervades Schelling's treatise.

Dieſes, wie [p. 287] geſagt, nicht greifliche und doch Allen empfindbare Weſen iſt es, was die Sprache der Griechen mit dem Namen der Chariß, die unſrige als Ahmuth be: zeichnet.“

Schelling determined the first relation such that not the dead reproduction of nature can be the essence of art, but rather the producing of the Idea that presents itself in nature. And likewise a merely mechanical equilibrium is by no means the ideal of art, but rather the measured taming of the life-filled urge — just as, in ethical matters, it is not the mere absence of passions that constitutes perfect character, but the wise mastery of desires and inclinations. Nature, like art, showed in its history precisely this progress from the shaping of the fermenting content into the severity of form, until at last, in perfect unity with it, the soul radiates through and through. In this section the most splendid depictions occur, for example: "In nature and art, essence strives first for the realization, or presentation, of itself in the particular. Hence the greatest severity of form shows itself in the beginnings of both: for without limitation the limitless could not appear; were there no hardness, mildness could not be, and if unity is to become perceptible, this can happen only through particularity, separation, and conflict. At the beginning, therefore, the creative spirit appears wholly lost in form, inaccessible, closed off, and even in greatness still harsh. But the more it succeeds in uniting its whole fullness in a single creature, the more it gradually relaxes its severity, and once it has fully developed the form, so that it rests satisfied within it and grasps itself — it becomes, as it were, cheered, and begins to move in gentle lines. This is the state of the most beautiful ripeness and bloom, where the pure vessel stands complete, the nature-spirit becomes free of its bonds, and feels its kinship with the soul. As through a gentle dawn-glow rising over the whole form, the coming soul announces itself: it is not yet there, but everything prepares itself, through the quiet play of delicate movements, for its reception. The rigid outlines melt and soften into gentle ones. A lovely being, neither sensuous nor spiritual but ungraspable, spreads itself over the form, and nestles into every contour of every movement of the limbs. This — as said, ungraspable yet felt by all — is what the language of the Greeks designates by the name Charis, and ours as grace."

Gegen das Ende der Abhandlung ſpricht Schel: ling ein wenig von dem Unterſchied der Plaſtik und Malerei und will an der Geſchichte der Italieniſchen Malerei ein Beiſpiel ſeiner Theorie des Entwickelungs ganges der Kunſt geben, wobei ihm Winkelmann's Unterſcheidung des ſtrengen, hohen und reizenden Style als Muſter diente.

Toward the end of the treatise Schelling speaks a little of the difference between sculpture and painting, and wishes to give, from the history of Italian painting, an example of his theory of the developmental course of art, taking Winckelmann's distinction of the severe, the high, and the pleasing style as his model.

Die Theorie :Schellings iſt darin, daß er den ſtrengen Styl von dem anmuthigen sondert, nicht falſch. Aber darin ist sie eß, daß ſie die Seele, wie er ſich ausdrückt, als eine zwar nicht bö bere, aber neue Stufe. der Kunſt regen will. Denn ſtatt [p. 288] Seele hatte er das Reizende als die Wiederauf:

According to his theory, Michelangelo was to have the character of severity, Correggio and, even more, Raphael that of grace, Guido Reni that of soul. Schelling here excuses himself by saying that, while this may not correspond exactly in chronology, it does so in substance; but in the fourth note he also wants to justify the matter chronologically, because although Michelangelo painted the Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel only after Raphael's death, his style had already been born before him and alongside him. Schelling's theory is not wrong in that it separates the severe style from the graceful one. But it is wrong in that it wants to see soul, as he puts it, as a new — though not higher — stage of art. For instead of soul he ought to have recognized the pleasing/charming as the dissolution

Isſung der erreichten idealiſchen Sobnheit erkerinen müssen. Schelling ſagt ganz richtig, daß die Kunſt auf ihrem Gipfelpuncte die früheren Momente, na: türlid als bloße Bildungsmomente, wieder durchlaufe. Eben ſo aber iſt es nothwendig, daß die Kunſt, nach: dem ſie ihren Gipfel erreicht bat, in dem Fortſchritt, der die Geſchichte ihres Unterganges einleitet, diesel: den Momente, jedoch in einer umgekehrten Mo: dification darſtellt. . Das einfach Erhabene wird zum Coloſſalen; die Grazie fängt an.coquett zu wer: den; die naive Nothwendigkeit der Erſchöpfung eines Vorwurfs wird zur Berechnung und Anbäufung der verſchiedenen Möglichkeiten, die er der verſtändigen Beziehung darbietet. Gewagte Stellungen, Fülle und Mächtigkeit der Glieder, Der: wickelung der Gruppen, mannigfacher Contraſt der Ge: ſtalten, reizten ihn. Correggio war deshalb ſein wahr: bafter Gegenſaß, in welchem, wie in Angelo die Große in Erhabenheit, ſo die Anmuth in die Zerfloffenheit überzuſpielen anfing. Correggio liebt, wie gerade ſeine berühmteſten Werke, ſeine Jo,. Antiope, Leda, zeigen, ungewöhnliche Stellungen, aber liebliche, ſanftſchwel: lende, jüße Formen, dámmerungslüchtige Beleuchtun: gen. Wollte Schelling, nach dieſen Malern noch ei: nen nennen, welcher Seele in der Bedeutung eines in ſich glühenden und doch ſtets gehaltenen Lebens aus: ſtrahlt, ſo mußte er Titian nennen, von dem er ganz ſchweigt. Titian wird gewöhnlich viel zu einſei: tig nach ſeinen Venusbildern und etwa noch nach ſeis nem- Christo della moneta in Dresden, beurtheilt. Wer aber die Bilder aus der Leidensgeſchichte von ihm im Belvedere geſehen hat, der wird wiſſen, welch ' einer Tiefe des Gemüths in den höchſten Sphären Rosenkranz Schelling.

back down of the ideal beauty that had been attained. Schelling says quite correctly that art, at its summit, runs back through the earlier moments — naturally as mere moments of formation. But it is just as necessary that art, after reaching its summit, in the further progress that inaugurates the history of its decline, presents these same moments, but in an inverted modification. The simply sublime becomes the colossal; grace begins to become coquettish; the naive necessity of exhausting a subject becomes the calculation and accumulation of the various possibilities it offers to the understanding relation. And so Schelling's example was bound to prove inadequate as well. Instead of Michelangelo he ought to have looked at the earlier painters Giotto, Orcagna, Cimabue, Perugino, Fiesole — and above all, if he wanted to name one all-encompassing name, Leonardo da Vinci, whom he presents as a transitional stage from Michelangelo to Correggio. With Vinci the striving for severity, for precision of form, came to a close. With him harshness softened in every direction. Raphael, however, whom Schelling also calls a philosopher and poet — which Michelangelo, in the proper sense of the word, was in a higher degree — was not only graceful but also soulful; and, half in jest, one might cite as proof that he indeed painted, unsurpassed, the story of Psyche. Michelangelo, for his part, already went beyond the soft ideal forms; he already passed over into the athletic. Daring postures, fullness and power of the limbs, entanglement of groups, manifold contrast of figures — these attracted him. Correggio was therefore his true opposite, in whom, just as in Angelo greatness began to shade over into the colossal, grace began to shade over into a melting dissolution. Correggio loves, as precisely his most famous works — his Io, Antiope, Leda — show, unusual postures, but lovely, softly swelling, sweet forms, twilight-toned lighting. If Schelling wished to name, after these painters, one more who radiates soul in the sense of a life glowing within itself yet always held in check, he would have had to name Titian, of whom he says nothing at all. Titian is usually judged much too one-sidedly by his Venus pictures and perhaps also by his Christ of the Tribute Money in Dresden. But whoever has seen his pictures from the Passion story in the Belvedere will know to what depth of feeling, in the highest spheres, [Rosenkranz, Schelling —] 19 Schelling's Later Period

p. 290

[p. 290] Titian fähig geweſen. Was iſt doch Guido Reni dagegen! Schelling preiſt das Bild, die Apotheoſe Maria's in München, als ein Aeußerſtes der Kunſt.

Titian had been capable. What is Guido Reni next to that! Schelling praises the picture of the Apotheosis of Mary in Munich as an extreme achievement of art.

Und gewiß unter den Bildern Guido's iſt es vielleicht ſeine größte Leiſtung. Darüber kann ich nicht ab: urtheilen. Sonſt aber ſcheint mir dieſer Maler, dem man das Eklektiſche, Akademiſche, Erfindungsloſe, im Colorit namentlich Unſichere, bei aller Feinbeit der Compoſition, ſchon ſo ſehr abmerkt und der auf mich in der Malerei gerade denſelben Eindruck gemacht bat, ' wie unter den Römiſchen Dichtern Claudianus im Raub der Proſerpina, das Prádicat der Seele gar nicht zu verdienen. Verſtändig iſt er und ſentimental. Schelling rühmt an ſeinen Fleiſætönen die Zartheit und erinnert dabei an den Italieniſchen Ausdruck morbidezza. Inſofern damit eine idealiſche Durchfich: tigkeit des Fleiſches ausgedrückt ſein ſoll, kommt dies ſelbe bei Correggio (außerdem bei Murillo) in ganz anderer, wahrhafter Weiſe vor.

And certainly, among Guido's pictures, it is perhaps his greatest accomplishment. On that I cannot pass judgment. Otherwise, however, this painter — in whom one already notices so strongly the eclectic, the academic, the lack of invention, and, for all the refinement of his composition, a particular unsureness of coloring, and who has made on me, in painting, exactly the same impression as Claudian, among the Roman poets, in the Rape of Proserpina — seems to me not to deserve the predicate of "soul" at all. He is intelligent and sentimental. Schelling praises the delicacy of his flesh-tones and recalls in this connection the Italian expression morbidezza. Insofar as this is meant to express an ideal translucency of the flesh, this same quality occurs in Correggio (and also in Murillo) in a quite different, genuine way. In Guido Reni the tints often already shade over into the sickly, the greenish, just as Rubens likes to apply such tones to the possessed.
